passage: Note from the art teacher, Friday. Kashish had a tray of paints that several children wanted. A boy in a red shirt held out a crayon and said, "You can use this. Can I use your paints?" Kashish smiled and slid the tray over. Chetan had been watching from the end of the table. He picked up his green crayon, walked round and held it out. "You can use this. Can I use your paints?" Kashish smiled again and made room. I said nothing and just watched. Mr Ali

qa.q: What did Chetan hold out to Kashish?
qa.a: Chetan held out his green crayon.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling while he watched from the end of the table?
qa.a: Chetan was eager and probably a little unsure how to ask. He learned by watching the boy in the red shirt first.

qa.q: What could Chetan try if Kashish had said no, and why?
qa.a: He could ask another child, or wait for a turn. A second plan means one no does not end it.

qa.q: How does the offer look to Kashish?
qa.a: Kashish gets something back, so sharing feels fair. Smiling twice shows the trade is welcome.

grounding: A child copies another child who trades a crayon for a turn with the paints, and it works.
